analytic.title: Work-in-Progress: A Timing-Anomaly Free Dynamic Scheduling on Heterogeneous Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Heterogeneous systems commonly adopt dynamic scheduling algorithms to improve resource utilization and enhance scheduling flexibility. However, it may introduce timing anomalies, wherein locally reduced tasks' actual execution times can lead to an increase in the overall system execution time. This phenomenon significantly complicates the analysis of Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT), rendering conventional analysis either overly pessimistic or unsafe, and often necessitating exhaustive state-space exploration to ensure correctness. To address this challenge, this paper presents the first timing-anomalyfree dynamic scheduling algorithm for heterogeneous systems, referred to as Deterministic Dynamic Execution. The core idea is to apply deterministic execution constraints, which partially restrict the resource allocation and execution order of tasks at runtime. It achieves a safe and tight WCRT through a single offline simulation execution. In this paper, we provide preliminary experimental validation of the timing-anomaly-free property of our algorithm and outline the basic idea of a formal proof.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Heterogeneous multi-core systems have gained more attention in emerging embedded systems with high computational demands and real-time requirements. Compared to homogeneous systems, these platforms integrate diverse types of processing units, enabling higher degrees of parallelism and improved resource utilization. However, the heterogeneity of resources and variations in execution behavior introduce significant challenges for task scheduling and WCRT analysis.

In these systems, scheduling is performed by either static or dynamic approaches. Static scheduling [1], where decisions such as assigning jobs to fixed cores are made at design time, enables precise WCRT analysis but sacrifices flexibility. Dynamic scheduling [2], [3] makes decisions at runtime, making it better suited to the resource variability and execution variability of heterogeneous platforms. However, dynamic scheduling may introduce timing anomaly (TA) [4], [5]. It is a situation where a locally shorter execution time leads to a globally longer execution time, which may lead to two problems. First, it may cause WCRT analysis to be unsafe, which is estimated via offline simulation using worst-case execution time (WCET) may be exceeded by the result of online execution without WCET. Second, it complicates the accuracy of WCRT analysis, which may require exhaustive exploration of all execution time combinations across heterogeneous units, leading to state space explosion.

However, existing research on TA mainly focuses on homogeneous systems. These works [6]- [9] primarily propose some dynamic scheduling algorithms that are TA-free and formally prove it. The core idea is to constrain the online execution, including the order or priority for tasks. However, extending these methods to heterogeneous platforms is nontrivial due to several challenges: First, dynamic scheduling on heterogeneous platforms introduces greater uncertainty. Since a task can be assigned to different heterogeneous processing units, it may have multiple WCETs. Therefore, existing constraints may not be sufficient to eliminate TA in heterogeneous scenarios. So it is necessary to develop new constraints and design corresponding TA-free dynamic scheduling algorithms. Second, it is challenging to formally verify that the proposed scheduling algorithm can guarantee TA-free. This is because it cannot be validated purely through experiments like simulation execution across all possible systems, including different task sets with various tasks and heterogeneous resource configurations. Therefore, a rigorous formal proof is the only viable approach to establishing this guarantee.

To address the above challenges, we try to propose execution constraints to eliminate TA for heterogeneous systems and their corresponding TA-free dynamic scheduling algorithm. Specifically, we design a constraint called the Deterministic Execution Constraint. It enforces task online execution with partial restrictions on resource allocation and execution order. We employ a delay execution mechanism to implement the constraints, thereby achieving the TA-free dynamic scheduling algorithm-Deterministic Dynamic Execution (DDE). In this WIP paper, we have preliminarily validated through experiments that the proposed algorithm is TA-free under certain system configurations. However, to rigorously establish that the algorithm is TA-free in arbitrary systems, a formal proof is required. At present, the corresponding proof has been largely completed, and this paper only outlines its core idea and overall process. The proof framework is primarily inspired by the formal proof of the TA-free processor (SIC) [10]. The experimental results initially indicate that, compared with existing heterogeneous scheduling algorithms, our algorithm can effectively reduce the WCRT of the system.

div.head: II. PRELIMINARY A. Heterogeneous System and Typed DAG
div.p: In this work, we study a generalized heterogeneous computing system that consists of multiple types of processing units, including CPU, GPU, and NPU. Different types of processing units exhibit distinct performance characteristics. The execution times of a task may vary across different types of processing units. To represent computing units uniformly, we use the notation X Z Y , X denotes the type of processing unit (e.g., CPU, GPU, NPU); Y indicates the specific model within that type, which may vary in processing capability (e.g., CPU 1 is a high-performance core, and CPU 2 is a low-power core); Z represents the instance label of that model.

Heterogeneous systems are often modeled as typed directed acyclic graphs (DAG). A typed DAG task set T d is represented as G = (V, E, G, τ ), where: V is the set of vertices, each representing a task; E ⊆ V × V is the set of directed edges, where (u, v) ∈ E indicates that task u must complete before task v can begin (i.e., a precedence constraint); M : V → 2 CU \ ∅ is a mapping from each vertex v to a non-empty set of computing unit types M (v) ⊆ CU , where CU is the set of all available computing unit types;
div.formula: τ : V × CU → I >0 is the execution time interval function, where τ (v, cu) = [BCET (v, cu), W CET (v, cu)] denotes the possible execution time interval of task v on a processing unit of type cu ∈ M (v).
div.p: As shown in Fig. 1, it is a typed DAG. The configuration of processing units is illustrated in the upper-left corner, and the execution time of each node on the corresponding processing unit is indicated below the node. Nodes in the DAG without incoming edges are referred to as source nodes, denoted by v src , and nodes without outgoing edges are referred to as sink nodes, denoted by v sink . The dependency relationships between tasks are defined by directed edges. Tasks are event triggered, which means a task can be executed only after all of its predecessor tasks have completed.

For a task v i of a node, let its start time be denoted as s vi and its finish time as f vi . The response time of task v i , denoted as RT (v i ), is defined as the time interval from the start time of the source node to the finish time of v i , i.e., f vi -s vsrc . If the DAG contains multiple source or sink nodes, a virtual source node is added to connect all source nodes, and a virtual sink node is added to connect all sink nodes. The response time of a DAG is given by RT (v sink ). The WCRT of a DAG is max π∈Π RT (v π sink ), where Π denotes the set of all feasible scheduling scenarios at a specific scheduling algorithm with variations in execution times for tasks.

div.head: B. WCRT Analysis Based on Simulation Execution
div.p: WCRT is typically obtained through offline simulated execution, in which each task is assumed to execute with its WCET. To illustrate this process, we consider the DAG shown in Fig. 1 and employ the HBFS (Heterogeneous Breadth-First Scheduling) algorithm. HBFS is the heterogeneity-aware Fig. 3. An example of TA: in this scheduling instance, not all tasks execute by their WCET; however, its response time exceeds that obtained in Fig. 2(b).

extension of the traditional BFS strategy [6]. It prioritizes tasks that are closer to the source node in the DAG and prefers processing units with higher speeds during allocation. Fig. 2(b) illustrates the results of an offline simulated execution by HBFS for the DAG in Fig. 1, where all tasks are assumed to execute with their WCET on the corresponding processing units. The observed finish time is 18.

However, during actual online execution, the execution time of tasks does not necessarily always reach their WCET. This uncertainty may lead to variations in scheduling behavior, such as changes in the set of tasks in the ready queue or in the availability of resources, thereby giving rise to multiple possible scheduling sequences. As shown in Fig. 2(a), which presents an online execution instance of the same system, but some tasks execute with durations shorter than their WCETs. This execution instance's finish time is 15, which is shorter than the offline WCET-based response time of 18.
Therefore, adopting the response time obtained from offline simulated execution as the system's WCRT appears to be a reasonable and safe choice.

div.head: III. A CASE FOR TIMING ANOMALY
div.p: However, the above method may not always yield a safe WCRT. Its validity relies on the assumption that using local WCETs can lead to the global WCRT. However, for nonpreemptive dynamic schedules like HBFS, which is locally greedy, this assumption often does not hold. TA is a counterintuitive phenomenon that tasks executing for less than their WCETs may actually lead to a longer system response time than obtained when all tasks execute with their WCETs.

Here, a TA phenomenon is illustrated through the example shown in Fig. 3. It is another execution instance for the same system in Fig. 2, whose response time is 20.5, longer than 18 obtained through WCET-based execution for all tasks in Fig. 2(b). In this case, tasks t 2 and t 4 execute with durations shorter than their WCETs used in the offline execution.

Even under conservative assumptions in offline simulation, TA may still occur. Specifically, suppose that each task, during offline execution, is assigned its WCET across all possible processing units in the system. This is equivalent to degrading each type of processing units to the slowest model within that type-for instance, treating all faster processors CP U 0 in Fig. 1 to the slower one CP U 1 . Under this assumption, the response time is 20. Nevertheless, a TA may still arise, yielding it is smaller than 20.5 in Fig. 3.
Therefore, under the influence of TAs, it becomes challenging to perform a sound and reliable analysis of the WCRT in heterogeneous systems with dynamic scheduling.

IV. DETERMINISTIC DYNAMIC EXECUTION To address this issue, we propose a TA-free dynamic scheduling algorithm, termed Deterministic Dynamic Execution (DDE). DDE operates in two phases: first, it derives deterministic execution constraints and the WCRT in the offline stage; second, it performs online dynamic scheduling with the predefined constraints.

The constraints consist of the following two aspects: Constraint 1(Resource Allocation Determinism): Tasks must follow a predetermined resource allocation pattern resAlloM ode D , where each pair (t 1 , res 1 ) indicates that task t 1 is only allowed to execute on computing units with the same X and Y of res 1 during online. This constraint restricts tasks from choosing computing units with different execution speeds, but not the same speeds.

resAlloM ode D = {(t 1 , res 1 ), (t 2 , res 2 ), ..., (t n , res n )} Constraint 2 (Execution Order Determinism): Tasks are required to start execution following a predetermined legal schedule order O D . The relation ⪯ denotes the execution order between tasks, where t 1 ⪯ t 2 means that task t 1 must begin execution no later than task t 2 . A legal order implies that the execution order satisfies all tasks' dependencies in a DAG.

O D = (t 1 ⪯ t 2 ⪯ t 3 ... ⪯ t N ) The above execution constraints are enforced through a delay-execution mechanism by global scheduling decisions. When determining whether to allocate computing resources and initiate the execution of a task, the following conditions must be simultaneously satisfied: (1) A suitable computing resource that meets the task's predetermined requirements resAlloM ode D ; (2) The task's predecessor tasks in the execution order O D must have already started execution. If either condition is not met, the execution of the task will be delayed until both conditions are fulfilled.

The construction of execution constraints can be achieved in two ways. (i) One may design a heuristic algorithm that searches for suitable resource allocations and execution orders with the objective of minimizing the WCRT. (ii) The constraints can be directly extracted from the WCET-based simulation results of existing dynamic scheduling algorithms.
For simplicity, we adopt the latter approach here. As an example, extract the resAlloM ode D and O D generated by HBFS under WCET execution, as illustrated in Fig. 2(b). The O D is:

And the resAlloM ode D is: (t 1 , CP U 0 ), (t 2 , CP U 0 ), (t 3 , CP U 1 ), (t 4 , GP U 1 ), (t 5 , GP U 1 ), (t 6 , GP U 0 ), (t 7 , CP U 0 ). Under these constraints, the system's WCRT is 18, which corresponds to the response time shown in Fig. 2(b).

As shown in Fig. 4, TA in Fig. 3 is eliminated under the above constraints. Specifically, after task t 2 finishes, task t 4 could have been scheduled on GP U 0 0 , but due to the constraint on execution order, it must wait until t 6 starts executing before it is allowed to begin. Moreover, t 4 is constrained to execute on instances of computing units type GP U 1 . As a result, its execution is delayed until time 5. It is noteworthy that, unlike static scheduling, our constraint does not enforce tasks to execute on a specific instance of a processing unit.

div.head: V. PRELIMINARY EXPERIMENTAL VALIDATION TA-FREE
div.p: Here, we preliminarily validate that our DDE is TA-free by performing numerous simulated executions.

div.head: A. A Case Study on Eliminating TA in a Fixed DAG
div.p: We first analyze a DAG system, as illustrated in Fig. 5(a). The system is initially scheduled using another online dynamic scheduling algorithm HFCFS, which prioritizes the earliestready tasks and allocates them to processors with higher processing speeds. The distribution of the system's online execution times is depicted in the first blue box of Fig. 5(b).

From the WCET-based simulation results of HFCFS, the corresponding bound W CRT HF CF S1 is 119. In addition, a more conservative offline bound, denoted W CRT HF CF S2 129, is obtained by the method described in Sec. III. We can find that the observed maximum (M SW CRT HF CF S ) online execution is 139, which exceeds both W CRT HF CF S1 and W CRT HF CF S2 , thereby confirming the presence of TAs.

Next, we apply DDE using the constraints constructed from HFCFS, denoted DDE HF CF S , following the construction method in Sec. IV(ii). In this case, the bound is W CRT DDEHF CF S which is equall to W CRT HF CF S1 = 119. The corresponding results, shown in the orange box plot of Fig. 5(b), clearly demonstrate that the execution time never exceeds 119. Therefore, no TA arises under DDE HF CF S . B. Validation with Randomly Generated DAGs 5,000 DAG systems were generated using a modified version of RDGEN [11] (extended to typed DAGs). For each system, 10000 simulated executions were performed. The DAG generation parameters are as follows: the G(n, p) model was used, with the number of nodes ranging from 20 to 30, and the edge probability p randomly selected within the interval (0.1, 0.7). The execution time of a node in the corresponding execution unit is [C min , c max ], where C min = rand [1,1000], C max = rand(x 1 , x 2 ) × C min there are 80% of nodes that use x 1 = 10, x 2 = 30 and the remaining nodes use x 1 = 1, x 2 = 1.2. There are four computational resource models: CP U 0 , CP U 1 , GP U 0 , GP U 1 . Configurations 1, 2, and 3 consist of 1, 2, and 4 instances of each model, respectively. Fig. 5(c) reports only the results of systems with TAs. Therefore, both W CRT HF CF S /M SW CRT HF CF S and W CRT HBF S /M SW CRT HBF S are less than to 1, indicating TAs. After applying our DDE, all TAs are eliminated, i.e., W CRT DDEHF CF S /M SW CRT DDEHF CF S and W CRT DDEHBF S /M SW CRT DDEHBF S are greater than or equal to 1. Theoretically, the two ratios should be 1, although the worst-case value may not be observed during 10000 times of online execution. Furthermore, it can be observed that if M SW CRT HF CF S and M SW CRT HBF S are coarsely regarded as the actual WCRT of HFCFS or HBFS, then the application of DDE reduces the WCRT, as reflected by W CRT DDEHF CF S /M SW CRT HF CF S and W CRT DDEHBF S /M SW CRT HBF S , both being less than 1. No TAs were observed for the HBFS under configuration 3.

VI. CORE IDEA AND PROOF OUTLINE OF TA-FREE Since it is infeasible to exhaustively enumerate all possible execution sequences in all systems, the above experiments can only provide preliminary evidence that the DDE algorithm may be free of TAs in certain systems, but cannot guarantee absolute safety. Therefore, it is necessary to formally prove the TA-free property of DDE. This formal proof has been largely completed, and in this paper, we only outline the main idea. The key insight is to demonstrate that, once deterministic execution constraints are introduced, the system execution exhibits monotonicity. The proof proceeds as follows:

First, an execution-progress model, inspired by SIC processor [10], is constructed to describe the heterogeneous system executions and to define the ordering of execution progress, i.e., how far the system evolves within the same time.

Based on this model, we define strict TA. Traditional definitions [5] focus only on whether an anomaly occurs in the system's final completion state (i.e., the last task to finish); the strict definition strengthens the completion state of every task during the execution process. So if a system is free of strict TA, it is guaranteed to be free of normal TA as well.
We then prove that, under deterministic execution constraints, the system cannot exhibit strict TA. Consequently, traditional TAs do not occur either.

To establish the strict TA-free, two lemmas must first be proven under deterministic execution constraints: Lemma 1 (Forward Progress Property): The execution progress of the system strictly increases with each state transition. Lemma 2 (Monotonicity): For two system states, if their corresponding execution progress satisfies a given ordering, then this ordering is preserved as the system evolves forward.
Next, we prove the strict TA-free in a special case, namely when only the execution time of a single task is reduced.
Finally, we generalize the proof to the general case where the execution times of multiple tasks are reduced simultaneously by constructing some intermediate states.

VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK This paper, for the first time, introduces a timing-anomalyfree dynamic scheduling algorithm for heterogeneous systems. Through a simulated execution experiment, we preliminarily validate that the proposed algorithm can eliminate timing anomalies and, compared with existing dynamic scheduling methods, reduce the system's WCRT. In addition, we present the fundamental idea of a formal proof to further support the theoretical soundness of the algorithm.

For future work, we plan to complete the formal proof in order to establish a more rigorous and general theoretical framework. Moreover, we will design efficient heuristic algorithms to explore deterministic execution constraints, thereby further optimizing the system's WCRT.
